KP13 Generalized Linear Classifiers

Level: undergraduate, year 3

Pattern Recognition | Chapter 4, §4.12

Slides: read and download

Learning objectives

  • Explain why we lift first and then use a linear classifier, and how a nonlinear boundary in the original space becomes a plane in the new space.
  • Compute the weights of a generalized linear classifier by least squares (the normal equation) and handle several classes.
  • Explain how a generalized linear classifier differs from projection pursuit and from a multilayer perceptron, and the price of lifting.

KP13 Generalized Linear Classifiers

One-sentence summary: First send xxx to a kkk-dimensional space with a set of fixed nonlinear functions fif_ifi​, then design an ordinary linear classifier there; all the nonlinearity is carried by the fif_ifi​ and the discriminant function stays linear in the weights.

1. Sandwiched classes

Plain explanation: What if no straight line separates the data in the original space?

Example (one dimension, designed here): class A at x=−3,−2,2,3x=-3,-2,2,3x=−3,−2,2,3 and class B at x=−1,0,1x=-1,0,1x=−1,0,1. Any single threshold, in either direction, gets at most 5 of the 7 right (exhaustive program search). The reason is that A lies on both sides of B, so xxx alone cannot show it.

Figure lec05-kp13-sandwich: the two classes on a line and the best single threshold.

2. A new coordinate

Feature mapping: use a set of functions fif_ifi​ to replace xxx by new coordinates y=(f1(x),…,fk(x))y=(f_1(x),\dots,f_k(x))y=(f1​(x),…,fk​(x)). Here y=(x,x2)y=(x,x^2)y=(x,x2): A has y2=4,9y_2=4,9y2​=4,9 and B has y2=0,1y_2=0,1y2​=0,1, and one horizontal line y2=2.5y_2=2.5y2​=2.5 separates the two classes, a linear classifier in the new coordinates.

Figure lec05-kp13-lift: the points lifted to (x,x2)(x,x^2)(x,x2) and separated by one horizontal line.

3. Curved when seen back on x

Formal definition: the generalized linear classifier

g(x)=w0+∑i=1kwifi(x), g(x)=w_0+\sum_{i=1}^{k}w_if_i(x), g(x)=w0​+i=1∑k​wi​fi​(x),

lifts with fixed nonlinear fif_ifi​ and then designs an ordinary linear classifier; "linear" means linear in the weights wiw_iwi​. Here g(x)=−2.5+0⋅x+1⋅x2g(x)=-2.5+0\cdot x+1\cdot x^2g(x)=−2.5+0⋅x+1⋅x2, g>0g>0g>0 means A and g<0g<0g<0 means B; g=0g=0g=0 at x=±2.5=±1.58x=\pm\sqrt{2.5}=\pm1.58x=±2.5​=±1.58, A outside and B inside. A line (in general a hyperplane) in the new space is two points in the original space. Seen the other way round, if a nonlinear hypersurface g(x)=0g(x)=0g(x)=0 separates the classes in the original space, writing ggg as a linear combination of the fif_ifi​ is the classical interpolation and function-approximation problem (source).

Figure lec05-kp13-curve: g(x)=−2.5+x2g(x)=-2.5+x^2g(x)=−2.5+x2 and the seven points.

4. XOR once more

Add the coordinate y3=x1x2y_3=x_1x_2y3​=x1​x2​ and take g=x1+x2−2y3−0.5g=x_1+x_2-2y_3-0.5g=x1​+x2​−2y3​−0.5: (0,0)→−0.5(0,0)\to-0.5(0,0)→−0.5, (0,1)→+0.5(0,1)\to+0.5(0,1)→+0.5, (1,0)→+0.5(1,0)\to+0.5(1,0)→+0.5, (1,1)→−0.5(1,1)\to-0.5(1,1)→−0.5, so one plane separates the four points. KP02 combined two lines; here one fixed mapping and one plane do the job.

Figure lec05-kp13-xor: new coordinates and ggg of the four XOR points.

5. Computing the weights

Normal equation: the solution w=(ΦTΦ)−1ΦTtw=(\Phi^T\Phi)^{-1}\Phi^Ttw=(ΦTΦ)−1ΦTt that minimizes the squared error between Φw\Phi wΦw and the targets (+1+1+1 for A, −1-1−1 for B); each row of Φ\PhiΦ is (1,f1,…,fk)(1,f_1,\dots,f_k)(1,f1​,…,fk​) of one sample. For the seven points of section 1 the rows of Φ\PhiΦ are (1,x,x2)(1,x,x^2)(1,x,x2) and the solution is w=(−0.810, 0, 0.238)w=(-0.810,\,0,\,0.238)w=(−0.810,0,0.238); the sign of each of the seven ggg equals its target, so all seven points are right (program).

Figure lec05-kp13-fit: the ggg values of the seven points.

6. Concentric rings

A program generates two classes of 100 points each, the inner ring of radius about 1.0 and the outer about 2.2. Straight-line features [1,x1,x2][1,x_1,x_2][1,x1​,x2​] are right only 51% of the time, no better than guessing; quadratic features [1,x1,x2,x12,x22,x1x2][1,x_1,x_2,x_1^2,x_2^2,x_1x_2][1,x1​,x2​,x12​,x22​,x1​x2​] are 99.5% right, and g=0g=0g=0 is a circle of radius 1.71 in the original space, between the two rings (program). Common misconception: after lifting the boundary becomes a straight line. It is a plane in the new space and a circle back in the original space.

Figure lec05-kp13-rings: the concentric rings and the decision circle.

7. Several classes

For MMM classes design MMM weight vectors wrw_rwr​ and pick the class with the largest wrTy+wr0w_r^Ty+w_{r0}wrT​y+wr0​. Example (designed here): nine points in one dimension with classes 1, 2, 3 on the left, middle and right; one-hot targets, features (1,x,x2)(1,x,x^2)(1,x,x2) and a least-squares solution for three weight vectors: all nine right; with only (1,x)(1,x)(1,x) just 7 are right and the middle class is right only at x=0x=0x=0 (a three-way tie of 1/31/31/3 there, resolved to the middle class).

Figure lec05-kp13-multi: the three ggg curves and nine points.

8. Contrast: projection pursuit

Projection pursuit: g(x)=∑ifi(wiTx)g(x)=\sum_i f_i(w_i^Tx)g(x)=∑i​fi​(wiT​x); fif_ifi​ sees the projection of xxx on a direction wiw_iwi​, and direction and function are optimized together. Double www: a generalized linear ggg doubles exactly, while for projection pursuit (fff a sigmoid, input 1, w=1w=1w=1) f(2)=0.881f(2)=0.881f(2)=0.881, not 2f(1)=1.4622f(1)=1.4622f(1)=1.462, so it is not linear in www and needs a two-stage alternating optimization (source). If fif_ifi​ is fixed to a sigmoid it is a one-hidden-layer neural network, which multilayer perceptrons have replaced in practice. To remember: generalized linear = fixed mapping + learnable linear layer; multilayer perceptron = learnable mapping + learnable linear layer.

Figure lec05-kp13-pp: block diagrams of the two structures and the doubling test.

Extension: how many coordinates, practice and worked solution

How many coordinates: quadratic features of an lll-dimensional input are lll terms xix_ixi​, lll terms xi2x_i^2xi2​ and l(l−1)/2l(l-1)/2l(l−1)/2 terms xixjx_ix_jxi​xj​, k=l(l+3)/2k=l(l+3)/2k=l(l+3)/2 in all: 5 for l=2l=2l=2, 65 for l=10l=10l=10 and 5150 for l=100l=100l=100. Does lifting really help? The source answers with Cover's theorem (KP14); polynomial and RBF mappings follow in KP15 and KP16.

Figure lec05-kp13-count: the number of quadratic features (log axis).
